title: Elul: getting ready
hook: the shofar sounds on Elul mornings, and prayers for forgiveness begin

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shneur Zalman's parable. Your line was the king is in the field. What came to meet you where you were? Today, how the field gets noisy. Day six hundred forty-three.

A weekday morning in late summer. The service is ending, people are folding their prayer shawls, someone is already checking their phone. And then, from the front, a sound that cuts through everything: a ram's horn. A long, raw blast, then broken notes, then a long one again. It isn't a holiday. Nobody's celebrating. It's just an ordinary Tuesday in Elul. In many synagogues, this happens every weekday morning for a month.
screen: `A WEEKDAY, LATE SUMMER.` → `A RAM'S HORN CUTS THROUGH.` → `EVERY MORNING FOR A MONTH.`

segments.voice: In Ashkenazi communities, the shofar is blown after the morning service through most of Elul, though not on Shabbat and not on the day before Rosh Hashanah. It's a wake-up call, a month early. The great medieval teacher Maimonides wrote that the shofar seems to say: sleepers, wake up from your sleep; look at your deeds and return. Then come the selichot, the prayers for forgiveness. Selichah means pardon. Sephardi communities rise early and say them through the whole month of Elul. Ashkenazi communities begin later, usually on the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes around midnight, and continue until Yom Kippur. Either way, the heart of every selichot service is the same: the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. They come from the moment after the golden calf, when God passes before Moses and proclaims: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 17b, pictures God wrapping in a prayer shawl like a prayer leader and showing Moses this order of prayer, promising that whenever Israel recites it, they will be answered. So the selichot repeat it again and again. Why a whole month? The tradition notes that Moses went back up the mountain for a second set of tablets at the start of Elul, and came down forty days later, on what became Yom Kippur. The days of repair have a long history. Elul is the runway. You don't arrive at the Days of Awe cold.
screen: `THE SHOFAR, EVERY WEEKDAY MORNING.` · `SLEEPERS, WAKE UP.` · `SELICHOT: PRAYERS FOR PARDON.` · `THE THIRTEEN ATTRIBUTES.` · then, large: `THIRTY DAYS TO GET READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear a shofar, or a bell. If you can, find a recording of a shofar and play it now. If not, the bell at the start of this sit will do. Let the sound be a wake-up call. When it fades, ask yourself one honest question: what from this past year needs looking at? Don't solve it. Just let the question stand. If you pray, you can say the line from Exodus: merciful and gracious. The bell holds the time.
Selichot. Prayers for pardon, built around the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, said in the weeks before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Your line: thirty days to get ready. Today, write down one thing from this year you'd like to make right before the new one starts. Day six hundred forty-three.

Shofar in Elul: Ashkenazi custom, skipping Shabbat and Erev Rosh Hashanah; confirm.
Selichot timing: Sephardim all of Elul; Ashkenazim from the Saturday night before Rosh Hashanah (at least four days); confirm.
Moses ascending on Rosh Chodesh Elul and descending on Yom Kippur: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 46 / Rashi on Exodus 33:11; confirm.
